claims.text: Friction stir processing can restore the integrity of the damaged high-performance alloy component.
Friction stir processing forms a refined, recrystallized microstructure in the repair zone.
The refined, recrystallized microstructure avoids the hot-cracking problems associated with traditional fusion welding.
The component alloy is sensitive to melting-related segregation and hot cracking.
The component has service-induced damage such as microcracks or localized deformation.
A rotating non-consumable FSP tool locally stirs and plasticizes the damaged zone without melting it.
Keeping the repair temperature below the melting point prevents melting and solidification in the processed zone.
FSP produces a refined, recrystallized repair-zone microstructure that minimizes segregation.
FSP eliminates the formation of phases that are sensitive to hot cracking.
FSP induces severe plastic deformation and intense plastic flow while the material remains below its melting temperature.
The deformation and plastic flow promote dynamic recrystallization and homogenization.
Homogenization reduces localized elemental segregation that would otherwise contribute to hot cracking in fusion-welded repairs.
The FSP-repaired zone will have improved joint integrity and a lower hot-cracking risk than a traditional fusion-welded repair.
The fatigue resistance and fracture toughness of the FSP repair will be at least comparable to those of a traditional fusion-welded repair.
Traditional fusion-welding repair is prone to hot cracking because it involves melting, solidification, segregation, and thermal stresses.
FSP repair is limited to materials in which adequate stirring and recrystallization can be achieved without excessive residual stress.

contradictions.description: The intervention specifies a rotating tool, whereas the conditions state that the clamped workpiece is rotated under the tool. This creates ambiguity about which body rotates during processing.
